messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Hone Kaniela had always been a man of precision and control, traits that served him well in his decades-long career as an airline pilot. But it was on a fateful night 40 years ago, during his time as a combat pilot, that his life took a drastic turn. The sounds of helicopters and the eerie glow of instrument panels still haunted him to this day. It started with small things – the feel of a certain texture, like the worn leather of an old flight jacket, would send him back to that night in an instant. The same time of day, just before sunset, would make his skin crawl as he remembered the darkness closing in around their aircraft. And then there were the sounds – helicopters or aircraft taking off and landing would set his heart racing like no other noise could. These triggers had become more than just annoying reminders; they now put him immediately on edge, making it harder for him to feel safe at night. As he navigated his daily life, Hone found himself constantly scanning for exits in every room or building he entered, a habit that made his wife worry about his growing paranoia. Sudden movements by others would startle him, putting him instantly on guard, as if his body was perpetually ready to respond to the threat of attack. This constant state of vigilance took its toll – not only did it exhaust him but also reinforced his deep-seated fear that the world was indeed a treacherous place. But there were moments when the past came flooding back without warning. The memory of that night still felt like an alien thing, something that belonged to someone else rather than himself. Yet, remembering the terror he felt at the time brought it all rushing back – the sounds, the smells, and the taste of fear in his mouth. His wife had grown accustomed to seeing him zone out, lost in thought as if trapped in a nightmare from which he couldn't awaken. As these episodes accumulated, Hone began to believe there was something fundamentally wrong with him as a person. He felt defective, broken beyond repair – like the damaged aircraft that still haunted his dreams. The world seemed more menacing than ever before, and this realization made it harder for him to shake off the feeling of impending doom. He had lost count of the number of nights he lay awake, staring into the darkness, as the sounds and textures and smells came flooding back. He couldn't recall when he'd last felt truly happy; his life now was a never-ending cycle of fear, anxiety, and dread. Hone Kaniela's wife tried to reassure him that things would get better, but deep down, they both knew it wouldn't be easy – not as long as the memories lingered, and with them, the perpetual threat of being sent back into the abyss. The cumulative effect was stifling his life, eroding his confidence as a pilot. Simple tasks now felt Herculean; the thought of facing another takeoff or landing made him anxious about losing control. As Hone's fear tightened its grip on his daily existence, it had become increasingly clear that he could no longer navigate these feelings alone – and so, after years of trying to hold on, he finally reached out for help, hoping against hope that someone might be able to guide him through the darkness back into the light.
